problem:
Consider the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{x+y}-x-y}{x+y}.
$$

 
The general solution to this equation can be expressed in the form

$$
g(x,y)=C-x,
$$

where $C$ is a constant. What is $g(x,y)?$
worked_solution:
First, we make the substitution

$$
z=x+y.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=1+\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1.
$$

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-1 & =\frac{{e}^{z}-z}{z}\end{aligned}
$$

Expressing this equation in the form ${z}^{′}(x)=f(z)$ gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{e}^{z}}{z}.
$$

This differential equation is separable. So, we separate the variables and integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{z}{{e}^{z}}\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \int z{e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Using integration by parts on the left side,

$$
\begin{aligned}u=z & \,⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{-z} & \,⟹\,v=-{e}^{-z}\end{aligned}
$$

we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int z{e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -z{e}^{-z}+\int {e}^{-z}\,\text{d}z & =\int \,\text{d}x \\ -z{e}^{-z}-{e}^{-z} & =x+C \\ -{e}^{-z}(z+1) & =x+K \\ {e}^{-z}(z+1) & =C-x\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=-K.$

Finally, we write the equation in terms of $y$ and $x$ using our original substitution, as follows:

$$
{e}^{-x-y}(x+y+1)=C-x
$$

Therefore, $g(x,y)={e}^{-x-y}(x+y+1).$
